sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Sandbag Hip Thrust is a glute-focused exercise performed with the upper back supported on a bench and a sandbag loaded across the hips.

Driving the hips to full extension against the sandbag strongly activates the glutes through a long range of motion.

It is a joint-friendly, portable alternative to the barbell hip thrust and is excellent for glute hypertrophy and hip extension strength.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Directly targets the glutes through full hip extension
- Builds hip extension strength and power
- Low spinal load compared with squats and deadlifts
- Softer padding on the hips than a barbell
- Portable and home-gym friendly
- Easily scaled by changing sandbag weight
- Great accessory for squats, deadlifts, and sprinting

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Gluteus Maximus

Secondary: Hamstrings, Quadriceps, Core, Adductors

sections.heading: Set Up
sections.content:
1. Sit on the ground with your upper back against a bench or elevated surface.
2. Position the bench so it contacts just below the shoulder blades.
3. Place the sandbag on your lap, just above your hips.

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Plant your feet firmly on the ground, shoulder-width apart.
2. Shins roughly vertical when hips are extended.
3. Hold the sandbag with both hands to keep it stable.

sections.heading: Thrust
sections.content:
1. Drive through the heels to lift the hips toward the ceiling.
2. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top and finish with hips fully extended.
3. Keep the ribs down and torso in a straight line from shoulders to knees.

sections.heading: Return and Repeat
sections.content:
1. Lower the hips back down under control.
2. Keep the core braced throughout.
3. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Overextending the lower back instead of extending the hips
- Pushing through the toes rather than the heels
- Letting the knees cave inward
- Tucking the chin to the chest or flaring the ribs
- Using a sandbag that is too heavy and breaking form
- Incomplete lockout at the top
- Resting the bag too low on the thighs

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Sandbag appropriate to your strength level
- Sturdy bench or elevated surface
- Flat, stable training surface
- Athletic shoes with flat, stable soles
- Optional: Hip pad for extra comfort
- Optional: Mirror to monitor form

sections.heading: Bench and Sandbag Placement
sections.content:
1. Position the bench behind you and make sure it will not slide.
2. Sit with your upper back against the edge of the bench.
3. Place the sandbag in the crease of the hips, not on the thighs.
4. Hold the bag with both hands to stop it shifting during the rep.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
2. Torso: Ribs down, core braced, chin tucked slightly.
3. Back: Upper back supported, lower back neutral.
4. Hips: Bag loaded across the crease of the hips.
5. Head: Neutral, eyes up and slightly forward.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Barbell Hip Thrust: Heaviest loaded variation
- Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Free-weight variation
- Glute Bridge: Floor-based variation
- Single-Leg Hip Thrust: Unilateral variation
- Hip Thrust Machine: Machine-based variation
- Cable Pull-Through: Hinge-focused glute exercise

sections.heading: Sandbag Hip Thrust Variations
sections.content:
Sandbag Hip Thrust: Described here
Sandbag Glute Bridge: Floor-based variation
Single-Leg Sandbag Hip Thrust: Unilateral variation
Tempo Sandbag Hip Thrust: Slow eccentric for hypertrophy
Pause Sandbag Hip Thrust: Pause at lockout for more tension
Feet-Elevated Sandbag Hip Thrust: Longer range of motion

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Pain: Reduce range, avoid overextension
Knee Pain: Bring the feet slightly forward and reduce load
Hip Pinch: Adjust bag position and reduce depth
Bench Discomfort: Use a padded bench or add a pad
Bag Too Light: Add sand or upgrade to a heavier bag
Bag Too Heavy: Use a lighter bag or switch to a glute bridge
Beginners: Start with a bodyweight glute bridge
